definition: A numerical operation on sampled data used to change or select signal characteristics, such as reducing a frequency range or smoothing rapid variation. Its effects include timing and startup behaviour as well as amplitude changes.
An operation that maps an input sequence of samples to an output sequence. The operation can include stored history, such as a previous input or output.
example: A sensor smoother combines each new reading with earlier readings.

definition: A system that preserves weighted combinations: processing a weighted sum gives the same output as applying those weights to the separately processed outputs and adding them. Its initial-state assumptions must be included.
example: A fixed gain of two is linear; adding a fixed offset is not.

definition: The property that lets a linear system process a signal in separate weighted pieces and add their outputs to obtain the combined result. It allows an input to be analysed as a collection of impulses.
The property that shifting the complete input in time shifts the output by the same amount without otherwise changing it. The processing rule does not depend on absolute arrival time.
A system that preserves both weighted input combinations and time shifts. Under zero-state assumptions its output is the convolution of the input with its impulse response.
An initial condition in which all stored filter history is zero. It excludes an extra output contribution from earlier inputs or nonzero stored values.
A discrete sequence with value one at sample index zero and zero at every other index. Scaled and shifted copies can represent individual samples of any finite sequence.
The output of a system initially at rest when its input is a unit impulse. For an LTI system it describes how each input sample contributes to the output over time.
A system whose current output depends only on present and past inputs, not future inputs. A zero-state LTI system is causal exactly when its impulse response is zero at all negative indices.

A system that requires future input values for a current output. Such processing can be possible offline when an entire recording is available, even though it cannot be applied immediately to an unknown live future.

The operation that adds shifted, scaled copies of one sequence using the other sequence's samples as weights. It predicts a zero-state LTI system's output from its input and impulse response; finite records use zero extension rather than wraparound.

Output remaining after the final nonzero input because the filter retains earlier input influence. A finite FIR has a finite tail; an IIR generally has a theoretically endless tail, which need not decay if the filter is unstable.
A filter that gives equal weight to a fixed number of neighbouring samples. A causal version uses present and past inputs; a centred offline version can also use future inputs.

The temporary behaviour as a filter moves from its initial stored state towards its response to the new input. A constant input can produce changing early outputs because the history initially contains zeros.

The sustained response to a continuing sinusoidal input after startup contributions have died away. In a stable LTI filter it has the input frequency with an amplitude gain and phase shift, unless the output amplitude is zero.

A description of how an LTI filter changes sinusoidal amplitude and phase as a function of frequency. Steady-state interpretation requires the relevant response to exist, as it does for the stable filters used here.
The nonnegative ratio of steady output sinusoid amplitude to input sinusoid amplitude at each frequency. It is the magnitude part of a filter's frequency response.
The phase shift a filter gives a steady sinusoid at each frequency, expressed in radians or degrees. At an exact response zero the output amplitude is zero and its phase is undefined.
A frequency region intended to pass through a filter within specified gain tolerances. Naming the region alone does not state how much attenuation or ripple is acceptable.
A frequency region intended to be reduced by at least a specified amount. A practical stopband normally has small residual output rather than exactly zero response everywhere.
The frequency region between a filter's passband and stopband. Its width is part of the trade-off among selectivity, coefficient count, ripple and delay.

A filter intended to preserve a low-frequency passband and reduce a higher-frequency stopband. Its transition and gain tolerances must be specified; it cannot restore information already lost through aliasing.
A filter whose zero-state impulse response becomes exactly zero after finitely many samples. A direct FIR computes weighted sums of present and past inputs using a finite coefficient list.
A numerical weight in a filter calculation. FIR coefficients weight input samples; recursive filters also have coefficients governing remembered outputs.
One coefficient and its associated input-delay position in a direct FIR filter. A 31-tap FIR uses a coefficient list with 31 entries.
An FIR design approach that limits and shapes an ideal impulse-response sequence using a finite weighting window. The window and length influence the transition region and residual response ripple.
Scaling filter coefficients to meet a stated gain reference, such as an amplitude ratio of one at DC. Unity gain at one frequency does not imply unchanged amplitude at every frequency.
A finite weighting sequence shaped by a raised cosine with nonzero endpoints. SciPy's symmetric Hamming form is intended for filter design; its periodic form is intended for spectral analysis.

Variation of a filter's amplitude response within a region where a flatter response is desired. Ripple tolerances are part of a filter specification rather than an automatic property of every low-pass filter.

A phase response that follows a straight line with frequency on intervals where the response is nonzero, allowing possible sign-related phase jumps. Real symmetric FIR coefficients provide this structure and constant group delay away from response zeros.

A timing measure determined by how filter phase changes over a small frequency region. A causal real symmetric FIR has a group delay of half of one fewer than its tap count, in sample intervals, wherever the response is nonzero.
example: A symmetric 31-tap filter has a 15-sample group delay.

definition: A path that contributes present or delayed input samples to a filter's output. A direct FIR uses these input contributions without a previous-output feedback term.
A path that uses a previous output to help compute a new output. It can keep passing an input's influence forwards, creating a theoretically infinite impulse-response tail.
A filter whose theoretical impulse response does not end after a fixed finite number of samples. Feedback implementations can represent this continuing influence with a finite amount of state.

A simple recursive filter whose new output combines the current input with a weighted previous output. A positive memory weight below one, with a complementary input weight, gives a low-pass smoother with unity steady DC gain.

Stored information from earlier processing needed to continue a filter correctly. Its numerical representation depends on the implementation, so a library state is not generally identical to the last output sample.

The property that every input with a finite absolute-magnitude bound produces an output with a finite bound under stated system and initial-condition assumptions. It does not guarantee that a particular computer type can represent that bound.

A parameter describing a recursive filter's natural repeated behaviour. For the specific first-order recurrence that adds input to a multiplier times previous output, that multiplier is its pole; its magnitude must be below one for BIBO stability when the input weight is nonzero.

A result exceeding the finite numerical range of its representation. The outcome depends on the type and operation; a signed 16-bit NumPy array multiplication can wrap to an unintended negative value.
The difference introduced when an exact value is approximated by an available numerical representation. Repeated arithmetic and coefficient rounding can change the behaviour of an implemented filter.

An implementation that divides an IIR filter into a sequence of smaller sections, each involving at most second-order behaviour. SciPy recommends this structure for most general IIR filtering because it reduces numerical problems compared with a single high-order direct form.

A consecutive group of samples handled together by software. Splitting a sequence into blocks should preserve a sample-wise filter's output when state, order, coefficients and arithmetic are retained.

The elapsed time from a signal entering a processing pipeline to its corresponding output becoming available. Buffer collection, queues, computation, filter delay and hardware can all contribute, so block duration alone is not total latency.

The time available to complete a processing task while sustaining incoming data without a growing backlog or missed output deadlines. A regular block's sample duration gives an arrival interval, but a practical budget also needs margin for scheduling and other work.
The stream-time interval represented by a block's samples: block size divided by sample rate. This is an arrival interval, rather than a complete statement of input-to-output latency.
example: A block of 64 samples at 48000 samples per second represents about 1.33 milliseconds.

definition: A frequency marking a stated response convention near a filter's transition. The convention must be named: SciPy firwin uses the half-amplitude point, while some other design functions use a half-power point.
A discontinuity when describing filter phase, such as a pi-radian shift as a real zero-phase response changes sign across a zero. At the exact response zero, output phase itself is undefined.
An operation that outputs the preceding input sample, shifting a sequence later by one sample interval. Its initial-history and finite-record handling must be specified.

A policy selecting which positions of a full convolution are returned. Full, same and valid modes differ in retained length and alignment; a same-length result does not by itself establish causal timing.
Work associated with each processing call in addition to the arithmetic on its samples. Smaller blocks require more calls per second, so reducing buffering can increase this repeated work.

A combination of signal values with non-negative weights adding to one. Its value remains between the smallest and largest contributing values, which gives a simple bound for the normalised one-pole smoother.

A finite-width integer result that returns to the representable range after crossing an endpoint. For example, in a NumPy signed 16-bit array operation, doubling 20000 wraps to −25536 instead of representing 40000.
A frequency at which a filter's frequency response has zero magnitude, so a sustained sinusoid at that frequency is cancelled after startup. Its zero-amplitude output has no defined phase.
example: A two-sample equal-weight average cancels a sequence alternating between 1 and minus 1.

definition: The continuing influence of earlier samples on a filter's current output. An FIR can remember a finite input history; a feedback filter can retain past influence through stored outputs.
